title: Brent Breaks $100 as US Sinks Five Iranian Tankers; Diesel Crunch Deepens
subhead: Oil crossed $100 a barrel for the first time in nearly two months after US forces destroyed five Iranian crude carriers and Iran retaliated with ballistic missiles at a US base in Jordan. Meanwhile, the global diesel market tightened further, with refiners in India running at up to 108% capacity and industry leaders warning the worst of the fuel crisis is still ahead.

sections.heading: Brent Crosses $100 as US Sinks Five Iranian Tankers
sections.body:
Brent futures hit $100 early Wednesday for the first time in nearly two months after US Central Command destroyed five Iranian crude carriers, according to OilPrice.com. Four of the vessels — the M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1 and M/T Riesco — were sunk in the Gulf of Oman, while the M/T Derya was struck near Kharg Island. Centcom said the strikes were in response to the IRGC targeting a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles, a continuation of the policy Admiral Brad Cooper outlined Saturday: 'If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours.'

Iran retaliated by firing 20 ballistic missiles at US forces in Jordan, with Jordan's Armed Forces reporting it intercepted 18 of them and that the remaining two fell on unpopulated areas. At the time of writing, WTI traded at $94.54 and Brent at $99.89, both nearly $2 higher on the session; by Wednesday afternoon Brent had extended to $101.46 (+3.62%) and WTI to $96.44 (+3.67%), roughly $6 higher week over week. OilPrice.com also noted Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities are adding another major supply risk as fighting spreads across the region.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is now systematically destroying Iranian crude carriers rather than merely interdicting them, and Iran is responding with missile salvos at US forces — a direct escalation that has pushed the market's psychological $100 threshold and raised the risk premium on every barrel moving through the Gulf.

sections.heading: Ukraine Strikes Novorossiysk, Threatening Kazakh Oil Route
sections.body:
Ukraine hit infrastructure in Novorossiysk, Russia's key Black Sea oil terminal, with drones overnight Wednesday, killing four civilians and sparking a fire at a fuel oil terminal at the port, OilPrice.com reported, citing the city's mayor Andrey Kravchenko. Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert 'Magyar' Brovdi confirmed a strike on the naval base that destroyed Russian military vessels, including missile carriers.

The attack puts renewed pressure on the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), the 1,500-kilometer route that carries more than 80% of Kazakhstan's crude exports from the Tengiz field to Novorossiysk. International producers including Chevron and ExxonMobil rely on the route to move Tengiz production to global markets. Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the port and the nearby CPC terminal, and last week a massive drone attack on Russia's northern port of Ust-Luga also sparked a blaze at an oil export terminal.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine is systematically degrading Russia's export infrastructure on both the Black Sea and Baltic coasts, and the collateral risk to Kazakhstan's CPC route means Moscow's war is now directly threatening a major non-Russian supplier's access to world markets.

sections.heading: Diesel Crunch Set to Worsen, Industry Warns at APPEC
sections.body:
Industry officials gathered at the APPEC petroleum conference in Singapore warned the global diesel market has not seen the worst of its crisis yet, OilPrice.com reported. Vitol Group chief executive Russell Hardy said global fuel markets are 'very tight and inflexible' despite higher crude flows out of the Persian Gulf, adding: 'We're still not running enough refining capacity to prevent those draws, and we keep eating into the surplus that exists around the world.'

Only about 1 million barrels per day of the estimated 10 million bpd flowing out of the Strait of Hormuz are refined products — the rest is crude. Refinery capacity is constrained in the Middle East by Iranian strikes on refineries and the trickle of fuel flows through Hormuz, while Russian refining is severely restricted by near-daily Ukrainian drone strikes and Moscow has banned diesel exports until at least the end of September. US and other refineries have been running at maximum capacity this summer after delaying maintenance, but analysts doubt they can sustain those rates much longer.
sections.whyItMatters: The tightness is in refined products, not crude — and with refining capacity constrained in the Middle East and Russia, diesel cracks at record highs are feeding directly into inflation across the global economy.

sections.heading: India's Refineries Run at Up to 108% as Diesel Demand Surges
sections.body:
India's refineries have been running at 105% to 108% capacity utilization over the past six months as diesel demand soars and international fuel markets tighten amid the Middle East crisis, OilPrice.com reported, citing Nandakumar Pillai, a director at Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Limited (MRPL), speaking at APPEC. MRPL, which operates a 300,000 bpd refinery on Karnataka's coast, will continue running above 100% until March 2027, Pillai told Reuters.

All Indian refiners are currently prioritizing diesel production at the expense of jet fuel amid soaring domestic demand and a global middle-distillate supply crunch. Diesel cracks have hit all-time highs as supply remains constrained in the Middle East and Russia, and maximized runs elsewhere cannot offset the barrels lost to the US-Iran war and Ukraine's drone attacks on Russian refineries.
sections.whyItMatters: India, the world's third-largest crude importer, is running its refining system flat out and reallocating output toward diesel — a sign the fuel squeeze is now reshaping production decisions across Asia, not just in the conflict zone.

sections.heading: US Crude Stocks Edge Lower as SPR Draws Continue
sections.body:
The American Petroleum Institute estimated US crude inventories fell 300,000 barrels in the week ending September 4, following a 2.6 million barrel draw the prior week, OilPrice.com reported. Commercial crude inventories excluding the SPR have lost just over 48 million barrels over the last 21 weeks. Another 1.2 million barrels left the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, bringing total SPR holdings to 285.4 million barrels — 446 million barrels shy of maximum capacity and near the 250-300 million barrel operational minimum below which the reserve struggles to pump efficiently.

US production rose to 13.862 million bpd for the week ending August 28, up 423,000 bpd from a year earlier. Gasoline inventories fell 1.9 million barrels and were already 6% below the five-year average, while distillate inventories gained 2 million barrels but remained 14% below the five-year average heading into the reporting period.
sections.whyItMatters: The SPR is being drawn down toward its operational floor at the same moment oil crosses $100, leaving Washington with a shrinking emergency buffer just as the Gulf crisis escalates.

sections.heading: Google Bets €13 Billion on Finnish Nuclear to Power AI
sections.body:
Google will invest at least €13 billion ($15.1 billion) in Finnish AI infrastructure over 2027-2028 and has signed a 22-year power purchase agreement with Fortum for up to 50% of the output from the Loviisa nuclear plant — Google's first nuclear power contract outside the United States, the companies said Wednesday, as reported by OilPrice.com. The Fortum deal funds a life-extension program keeping Loviisa, which supplies about 10% of Finland's electricity, running through 2050; without it the plant would have shut after 2030. Fortum shares rose 10% within hours.

The buildout adds capacity at Google's Hamina data center campus and three new sites in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, and is part of Alphabet's global 2026 capital spending plan of $195-$205 billion. Google separately signed onshore wind contracts adding 629 megawatts and a 94-megawatt battery system near Kajaani. The deal joins Microsoft's 20-year, 835-megawatt agreement with Constellation to restart Three Mile Island Unit 1 and Amazon's 1,920-megawatt supply deal with Talen at Susquehanna.
sections.whyItMatters: Big Tech is now directly financing nuclear life extensions and new capacity on both sides of the Atlantic to secure baseload power for AI data centers — turning nuclear energy into a strategic asset in the AI race.

bottomLine: Oil crossed $100 for the first time in two months as the US escalated from interdicting to destroying Iranian crude carriers and Iran answered with missile salvos at US forces in Jordan, while Houthi attacks on Saudi facilities added further supply risk. Beneath the crude headline, the real stress is in refined products: diesel cracks are at record highs, India's refineries are running at up to 108% capacity, Russia has banned diesel exports, and industry leaders at APPEC warn the worst of the fuel crunch is still ahead. Ukraine's strike on Novorossiysk also put Kazakhstan's CPC export route back in the crosshairs. Separately, Google's €13 billion Finnish nuclear deal underscored how the AI boom is now reshaping power markets and nuclear diplomacy.
